html:
A popular uprising in the South Korean city of Gwangju in May 1980, crushed by the army. It began on 18 May when students protested against martial law, imposed after General Chun Doo-hwan took power following the murder of President Park Chung Hee in 1979.

Paratroopers beat and shot protesters. The city's people took arms from police stations, drove the troops out and ran Gwangju themselves for several days. On 27 May the army retook it. Official counts give about 200 dead; others put the toll far higher.

The government called it a communist revolt and censored the news. The memory of Gwangju fed the June Democratic Struggle of 1987, which won direct elections for president. In 1996 Chun was convicted of treason and for the massacre. The anniversary is now a national day, central to how South Korea tells the story of its democracy.
